📹 Albanese meets King Charles on sidelines of CHOGM
Prime Minister Anthony Albanese has had an encounter with King Charles on the sidelines of the CHOGM meeting in Antigua.
"[They] said today at my press conference, 'Why are you, why are you here?' Because His Majesty invited me," Albanese told the king.
"Oh God, it's all my fault, oh no," Charles replied.
📹 Is government spending to blame for inflation crunch?
Analysis: Interest rate hikes gather pace across the globe as deficits and debt spiral
It'll only take a few minutes from Michele Bullock's ascension to the podium at this afternoon's post-rate decision press conference for the blame game to begin.
Who is responsible for the inflation outbreak?
She won't answer, at least directly. And she certainly won't deliver the answer required by a baying press pack.
For most of this year the opposition has cleverly sheeted responsibility home to the federal government with accusations of profligate spending.
It's not just gaining traction, it's become an article of fact.
Shadow Treasurer Tim Wilson is having a field day.

Treasurer Jim Chalmers, it is said, is out of control, spending your hard-earned tax dollars like a drunken sailor, pushing up the price of almost everything and forcing the Reserve Bank to counter with rate hikes.

NDIS changes must deliver savings, finance minister says
Finance Minister Katy Gallagher has been asked about doubts that NDIS changes will save the budget $38 billion as projected.
Speaking to ABC Canberra, Gallagher was adamant that those savings had to be found.

"Absolutely we have to deliver those savings," she said."Otherwise the social licence of the NDIS will start to disappear. It cannot keep growing at the speed with which it's growing and consume more and more of the budget."
"Absolutely we have to deliver those savings," she said.
"Otherwise the social licence of the NDIS will start to disappear. It cannot keep growing at the speed with which it's growing and consume more and more of the budget."
She said if the proposed changes to the NDIS didn't result in the expected billions, the disability agency would have to find another way.
Speaking on a day where interest rates are anticipated to rise again, Gallagher accused the opposition and the Greens of blocking legislation that would help the budget bottom line.

"Every time we bring savings, and even the NDIS — when we brought that legislation to the parliament, the Greens never backed it, the Liberals delayed it, that delay cost several hundred million dollars."
Key Event
Questions raised about whether the NDIS cuts will save government $38 billion
Significant changes to the National Disability Insurance Scheme, announced in April, were designed to deliver the government $38 billion in savings over the next four years.
But the Australian government's actuary, in his preliminary findings, has indicated it is not yet convinced the disability agency overseeing the scheme will be able to save that amount.
In a letter to the National Disability Insurance Agency in September, reviewing actuary Guy Thorburn said overall he thought the projections were in the "range of reasonably likely outcomes".

"[H]owever, there is considerable uncertainty regarding the actual level of future Scheme expenses," he wrote."There are some aspects of this projection which, I believe, may present additional risk that the actual Scheme expenses will exceed the projected expenses."
"[H]owever, there is considerable uncertainty regarding the actual level of future Scheme expenses," he wrote.
"There are some aspects of this projection which, I believe, may present additional risk that the actual Scheme expenses will exceed the projected expenses."
He noted implementing proposed changes "will require a significant level of resources over the short term" and has requested more information about the plans "underpinning the reforms".

The NDIS is one of the most-costly items in the budget, and Thorburn notes changes to the scheme are designed to improve financial sustainability by reducing expenditure growth by 5-6 per cent in the medium term.
Premier says SA will join Commonwealth defence of social media ban in High Court
SA Premier Peter Malinauskas says his state will join the Commonwealth and defend the under-16s social media ban in the High Court today.
The world-first social media ban will face its first major legal challenge from Libertarian NSW MP John Ruddick and the Digital Freedom Project, which is also suing the eSafety commissioner.
The ban came into effect in December last year and effectively blocked young Australians from creating or keeping a social media account.
Speaking to ABC News Breakfast, Malinauskas says the ban will help protect children from harm online and has rejects it will curtail free speech.

"The reason why we have these laws in Australia and the reason why now every month it feels like a new country is announcing they're going to do the same, it's because of the interests of children," Malinauskas says."This is about protecting children from a platform that we definitely know through peer reviewed research is doing them harm."

"The reason why we have these laws in Australia and the reason why now every month it feels like a new country is announcing they're going to do the same, it's because of the interests of children," Malinauskas says.
"This is about protecting children from a platform that we definitely know through peer reviewed research is doing them harm."
Gallagher refuses to say if Labor will aim for net savings in MYEFO
Finance Minister Katy Gallagher has refused to say whether the government will aim for net savings in the mid-year fiscal and economic outlook (MYEFO).
The Reserve Bank will announce its interest rates decision today, just a week after inflation jumped to 4.3 per cent in September.
Speaking to ABC AM program, Gallagher says the inflation challenge in Australia is driven in part by the Middle East war.
Asked if the government will seek to reduce spending, the finance minister says the Expenditure Review Committee is examining decisions.

"They need to be taken thoughtfully and carefully through our processes and they will be. But the treasurer and I and the PM have all flagged that there will be savings, and we've done that in every budget and every budget update," Gallagher says.
"We've repaired the budget. We've found those savings, and the deficit is much smaller than it was when we inherited it and that's the focus of our decision making."
Bragg defends early access to super for first home buyers
Andrew Bragg has pushed back on a Liberal backbencher's call to not allow first home buyers to access their super early to buy a home.
Liberal MP Garth Hamilton says he's confident he has convinced a majority of colleagues to rule out any early access for first home buyers.
Bragg, who has led the push for early access to super for first home buyers with Shadow Treasurer Tim Wilson, says people are "entitled to their views".

"What we want to try and do here is make sure that we align the housing systems with the retirement and super systems to ensure that we don't have a nation of retired renters and that's something that's under review at the moment," Bragg says.
"But we're going to hit one million retired renters over the next five years. That's going to mean there's going to be a lot of Australians that are going to have a very hard retirement."
Housing tax changes have 'destroyed' confidence: Bragg
Liberal frontbencher Andrew Bragg says the government's changes to capital gains tax and negative gearing have "destroyed" confidence.
Data from research group Cotality shows house prices have fallen for the seventh consecutive month — the fastest pace in 40 years.
Speaking to ABC Radio National Breakfast, Bragg says the changes have had an disproportionate impact on the housing market.
"No-one has won from these taxes and you can see it as measured in the data with higher rents, fewer houses being built, and fewer loans to owner-occupiers," Bragg says.
"So that has hurt the housing market massively because the last thing that market needed was more taxes. So, of course, it's had an impact overall on that system."
US midterm elections could have 'potentially big economic consequences': Chalmers
The US midterm elections are happening tomorrow, with control of all House of Representative seats and a third of Senate seats up for grabs.
Asked whether the result of the midterm elections could have an impact on inflationary pressures in Australia, Jim Chalmers says it probably would.
The treasurer has told ABC Radio National Breakfast the world would be watching "very closely" at the races.
"That's because there are potentially big economic consequences of these midterms, particularly when it comes to any implications for the war in the Middle East," Chalmers says.

"I think it's self-evident that the Americans are dealing with a lot of the same issues that we are, whether it be inflation or these other pressures on people. The difference between us and the Americans is that they have a say in when the war ends and we don't."
Chalmers says Labor is 'weighing up' savings measures
Treasurer Jim Chalmers hasn't given an indication about what savings the government will present in the mid-year fiscal and economic outlook.
The federal government is under pressure to cut back spending after inflation jumped last week and the Reserve Bank's interest rates rises.
Chalmers says the Expenditure Review Committee (the group advises cabinet ministers on budget spending) met yesterday and will meet again tomorrow.
Speaking to ABC Radio National Breakfast, Chalmers says if interest rates increase today, it will place further pressure on households.

"People are under substantial pressure already, and obviously, if rates go up today, that will make things much harder, especially when there are already a number of rate rises in the system and their full effect hasn't been felt yet," Chalmers says.
"We know that there is more work to do to make the budget as tight as it can be, weighing up all of the considerations and all of the pressures that we're dealing with right now"
Chalmers backs Treasury house prices forecasts despite fall in home values
Treasurer Jim Chalmers has backed Treasury forecasts showing a slight fall in house price value growth, following new data this week.

Its latest national Home Value Index (HVI) was down 1.2 per cent in October and is now 6.7 per cent below its March peak, equivalent to a decline of about $63,400 in the value of the median Australian dwelling.
Speaking to ABC Radio National Breakfast, Chalmers says "volatility" in the market is contributing to house prices.
"Well, the forecasts or the assumptions that are in the budget from the Treasury around house prices are about the next couple of years, not the last couple of months," Chalmers says.

"And so we're already seeing a fair bit of volatility in the housing market. There are a number of reasons for that. We've seen house prices come off more than half a dozen times in the last couple of decades."
Wilson stands by superannuation push despite colleague's resistance
Tim Wilson has pushed back on a Liberal backbencher's attempt to prevent his party from adopting a policy of allowing first home buyers to access their super early.
Liberal MP Garth Hamilton says he believes there's a majority in the party room who don't want to allow first home buyers to access their super early to purchase a home.
The idea has been floated by senior Liberals, including Wilson, as a solution to help younger Australians get into the property market.
Asked about Hamilton's push on ABC News Breakfast this morning, Wilson says the Coalition's position isn't to be changing super.
But he strongly suggested he's still in favour of allowing early access to super for purchasing a first home.

"I've said consistently that … the average age of Australian buying a home now is around 40. It's not quite there, but it's nearing there with a 30-year mortgage," Wilson says."That means that people are only going to be using super at the start of buying a home, or the end to pay off their mortgage."

"That means that people are only going to be using super at the start of buying a home, or the end to pay off their mortgage."
Wilson takes aim at government spending ahead of rates decision
Shadow Treasurer Tim Wilson has stepped up on ABC News Breakfast to discuss Australia's inflation and interest rates.
The Reserve Bank will announce its interest rates decision today, just a week after the announcement that inflation jumped to 4.3 per cent in September.
He says federal government spending is behind Australia's persistent inflation, saying it predates the war in Iran.

"We know that the Middle East is having an impact on a headline inflation, but that isn't the metric that the Reserve Bank uses, which is underlying inflation," Wilson says."Underlying inflation lifted above the RBA's target band in July of last year, so seven months before a single bomb was dropped on Tehran."
"We know that the Middle East is having an impact on a headline inflation, but that isn't the metric that the Reserve Bank uses, which is underlying inflation," Wilson says.
"Underlying inflation lifted above the RBA's target band in July of last year, so seven months before a single bomb was dropped on Tehran."
The Coalition has unveiled cuts to climate and housing initiatives, and plans to cut non-citizens from welfare and NDIS programs.
But asked if those cuts would also involve public service job cuts, Wilson said there would be if "bureaucracy exists and it's not serving a purpose".
Canavan under 'no illusions' about task to win seat of Capricornia
Nationals leader Matt Canavan says he's under "no illusions" about his efforts to win the federal seat of Capricornia.
Canavan put his hand up to contest the Central Queensland seat at the next election, after sitting MP Michelle Landry announced her intention to resign.
Yesterday, One Nation leader Pauline Hanson and party director James Ashby both ruled themselves out of contesting the seat, saying they would instead put forward another candidate.

"I'm under no illusions. You're not owed anything in this game. You've got to fight every day to represent the people. It's been a great honour to be a senator for Queensland," Canavan tells Channel Nine.
Antigua's PM lauds Australian 'leadership' at Commonwealth meeting
Anthony Albanese has met with Gaston Browne, prime minister of Antigua and Barbuda, on the sidelines of the Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting (CHOGM).
The host nation's leader applauded Australia's attendance at the biannual summit, which is the first time an Australian leader has visited the Caribbean in 17 years.
"We are looking forward to repositioning the Commonwealth as a more consequential grouping of nations," Browne said.
"I think with your leadership you can help make CHOGM a force for global good, stability and progress."
Following a major upgrade to Antigua's port, funded by China, Browne said he wanted his nation to become a "gateway for Australian products" into the Caribbean, including wine and beef.
Albanese in turn thanked Browne for his hospitality and said there was "much more we can do together" in relation to climate change.

"We have worked closely with our Pacific island friends on climate change, and we have some smaller islands as part of the Torres Strait that are impacted by rising sea levels.""There are a range of scientific breakthroughs we're able to help you with including … mapping of reef conditions and what the impact of climate change will be," he said.
"We have worked closely with our Pacific island friends on climate change, and we have some smaller islands as part of the Torres Strait that are impacted by rising sea levels."
"There are a range of scientific breakthroughs we're able to help you with including … mapping of reef conditions and what the impact of climate change will be," he said.
Both Albanese and Browne are on the record as wanting to make their nations republics. Browne has also called for reparations as a result of the transatlantic slave trade.

Asked if he supported calls for financial compensation from the UK, to affected nations, Albanese said he looked forward to "respectful discussions between the UK and the countries that are directly involved.
"Australia isn't a direct participant in those discussions, but we want to see them take place transparently and in a constructive way."
Key Event
Albanese defends economic record, ahead of RBA decision

Holding a snap pre-interest rate decision press conference in the Caribbean, the prime minister defended the government's economic policies ahead of what's likely to be the RBA's fifth interest rate hike this year.
"My government has made savings in every single economic statement," Anthony Albanese said.
"We work each and every day on cost of living."
Defending his decision to attend the Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting (CHOGM) in Antigua, the prime minister said it's important to "engage in the world".
"What I recognise as well is that by engaging in the world, we can deal with our national security interests, but also make our economy stronger," he said.
Albanese also denied criticising the Reserve Bank when he described interest rates as a "blunt instrument", the same language used by RBA governor Michelle Bullock.
PM urges Commonwealth to 'strengthen democracy,' as he makes UN pitch

In the wake of a violent attack on independent MP Helen Haines last month, the prime minister has told Commonwealth leaders it's not enough to celebrate democratic institutions, and urged greater action to "strengthen democracy" and protect elected representatives.

As official CHOGM talks got underway in Antigua, Anthony Albanese delivered a wide-ranging speech aimed at progressing Australia's bid for a temporary seat on the UN Security Council from 2029, where he outlined Australia's approach to addressing political violence and rising polarisation globally.
"We must assist smaller nations to develop the democratic, economic, social and climate resilience they need to build a peaceful and prosperous future," he said.

"Australia is responding to global uncertainty by amplifying the voices of small states and middle powers, working to prevent crises, resolve conflicts and protect civilians, and elevating relationships that help to build sovereign capability."
All 56 commonwealth nations are part of the UN General Assembly, and get to vote for non-permanent security council members.
The prime minister also highlighted Australia's role in the middle-power push to regulate artificial intelligence.
The motivations behind the attack on Haines are under investigation.
